title: Is Fairness Truly Fair? Towards Reliable Lipschitz Fairness in Multi-Task Learning via Fixed-$\delta$ Alignment

problem.claim: Lipschitz fairness evaluation in multi-task learning can be confounded by method-induced representation scales.

gap.claim: Deriving auditing tolerances from each model's representation distances causes algorithms to be compared under different semantic thresholds.

contributions.claim: ReLiF separates evaluation-time fixed-$\delta$ auditing from training-time controlled regularization.
The paper develops analyses of threshold drift, reference-tolerance selection, and the relationship between huberized and unsmoothed positive-margin training surrogates.
ReLiF uses a shared reference tolerance for comparable auditing and a violation-rate feedback controller to regulate the Lipschitz surrogate during stochastic training.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on clinical time-series benchmarks and NYUv2 show that fixed-$\delta$ auditing exposes utility-fairness trade-offs that method-dependent thresholds can obscure.
Using a ResNet50 backbone on NYUv2, ReLiF maintains competitive utility and markedly lowers aligned bias when evaluated with common fixed thresholds.
On clinical benchmarks, ReLiF yields controlled fairness-regularized trade-offs, while task-balancing baselines can sometimes achieve lower bias and utility-fairness trade-offs persist.

narrative_sequence.summary: Representation scales can confound Lipschitz fairness evaluation in multi-task learning.
Threshold drift can alter bias rankings, although sufficient conditions for preserving rankings are identified.
ReLiF combines fixed-$\delta$ auditing with controlled training-time regularization using a shared tolerance and feedback controller.
Additional analysis addresses threshold selection and training-surrogate behavior.
Experiments report that fixed-$\delta$ auditing reveals trade-offs and that ReLiF can reduce aligned bias while retaining competitive utility.

source_observation.claim: Model-dependent auditing thresholds can obscure utility-fairness trade-offs and change bias rankings.

interpretation.claim: Evaluation protocols should hold semantically meaningful tolerances fixed when comparing models.

application.claim: Use shared fixed-threshold auditing for comparable fairness evaluation across multi-task learning methods.

exception.claim: Task-balancing baselines can sometimes achieve lower bias, so fixed-threshold evaluation does not imply ReLiF is uniformly best.

source_observation.claim: A violation-rate feedback controller keeps the fairness surrogate active without allowing it to dominate stochastic training.

interpretation.claim: Feedback control may help balance fairness regularization against task utility during training.

application.claim: Consider adaptive regularization control when fairness objectives compete with primary learning objectives.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this control strategy generalizes beyond the reported multi-task learning settings.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the exact fixed-$\delta$ values or reference-tolerance selection procedure.
The abstract does not report detailed dataset sizes, metrics, baselines, or statistical results.
The abstract does not provide implementation details or independent verification.
